name: J. M. G. Le Clézio
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Prix Renaudot in 1963 for his debut novel Le Procès-Verbal (The Interrogation), published by Gallimard when he was 23.
early_history_summary: Le Clézio began writing as a child during a month-long voyage to Nigeria at age eight and never stopped. He studied at Bristol University and the University of Nice, completing his undergraduate degree in 1963, the same year his unsolicited manuscript was accepted by Gallimard and awarded the Prix Renaudot.
family_context_summary: Father was a medical doctor stationed in Nigeria during WWII; both parents had strong family connections to Mauritius. The family was of Breton origin with a middle-class professional background.
parent_family_domain_summary: No clear evidence of literary or publishing family background; father was a doctor, not in a literary domain.
primary_early_advantage_tags: early writing, bilingual, multicultural, professional family, French literary milieu
evidence_summary: Le Clézio began writing at age seven or eight during a voyage to Nigeria and continued writing throughout his childhood and adolescence. His father was a doctor, and the family had deep Mauritian-Breton roots, giving him a bilingual and multicultural upbringing. He sent his first novel as an unsolicited manuscript to Gallimard, which published it and saw it win the Prix Renaudot in 1963 when he was 23. No family literary domain advantage or inherited network is documented; his breakthrough appears largely self-created through persistent early writing.

name: Paloma Picasso
milestone_by_age_26: Launched her first collection of costume jewelry in Yves Saint Laurent's Rive Gauche boutiques in Paris in 1971 at age 22, after Saint Laurent commissioned her to design accessories for his collection.
early_history_summary: Growing up in Paris and the South of France immersed in art and culture as the daughter of Pablo Picasso and Françoise Gilot, Paloma developed an interest in design through flea-market finds and costume jewelry. After attending Université Paris Nanterre, she worked as a costume designer for the Folies Bergère, where her rhinestone creations drew critical attention and led to her commission from Yves Saint Laurent.
family_context_summary: Daughter of Pablo Picasso, one of the most famous artists of the 20th century, and Françoise Gilot, a painter and author. Grew up immersed in the Parisian art world with access to influential cultural figures.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Pablo Picasso was one of the world's most famous painters; mother Françoise Gilot was a painter and author. Direct family-domain advantage in art and design was immense, providing both inspiration and access to elite cultural circles.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Picasso daughter, art world, Paris, Yves Saint Laurent, family wealth, cultural elite
evidence_summary: Paloma Picasso was born into one of the most famous artistic families in the world as the daughter of Pablo Picasso and Françoise Gilot. She grew up in Paris and the South of France, immersed in art and surrounded by influential cultural figures. Her early jewelry creations from flea-market finds caught the attention of critics, and her friend Yves Saint Laurent commissioned her to design accessories for his collection, launching her first jewelry line in his Rive Gauche boutiques in 1971 at age 22. The family name, wealth, and network provided extraordinary access to the Parisian fashion and art world.

name: Jochen Mass
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Spa 24 Hours endurance race in 1972 and was crowned European Touring Car Champion that same year, both at age 25, driving a Ford Capri RS2600.
early_history_summary: Mass came to racing relatively late after working in the merchant navy and then as an apprentice at an Alfa Romeo dealership in Mannheim, where the owner recognized his talent and entered him in racing events. He moved up through Formula Super Vee, Formula Three, and European Formula Two, gaining international prominence in the European Touring Car Championship with Ford Capris in the early 1970s.
family_context_summary: Father's family came from Mecklenburg where his grandfather worked as a ship captain. Mass worked on merchant navy ships after leaving school, which started a lifelong passion for sailing. No family motorsport background is documented.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No family connection to motorsport or racing.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Alfa Romeo apprenticeship, Ford works team, late start, merchant navy, European motorsport
evidence_summary: Jochen Mass discovered racing relatively late after working in the merchant navy, starting an apprenticeship at an Alfa Romeo dealership in Mannheim where the owner recognized his driving talent. He progressed through hill climbs and touring car racing, earning a call-up to the Ford works team in 1970. By 1972 at age 25, he won the Spa 24 Hours and the European Touring Car Championship. No family motorsport background or financial support is documented; his entry into racing came through the dealership apprenticeship.

name: Patrick Modiano
milestone_by_age_26: Published his first novel La Place de l'Étoile in 1968 at age 22, which won both the Fénéon Prize and the Roger Nimier Prize.
early_history_summary: Modiano was introduced to the literary world by Raymond Queneau, his geometry teacher at Lycée Henri-IV and a friend of his mother. Queneau brought him to a Gallimard cocktail party where he met his future publisher. After reading his manuscript to Queneau, Gallimard published his debut novel in 1968, which won two literary prizes.
family_context_summary: Father Albert Modiano was of Jewish-Italian origin, involved in black market dealings during WWII; mother Louisa Colpeyn was a Flemish actress. Parents separated shortly after Patrick's birth. He was raised by maternal grandparents, learning Flemish as his first language. His younger brother Rudy died at age 9.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother was a Flemish actress with cultural connections, including friendship with Raymond Queneau. Father's wartime experiences and ambiguous moral position deeply influenced Modiano's literary themes, though no direct literary domain transfer is documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Queneau mentor, Gallimard, Paris, WWII themes, absent parents, brother's death, Lycée Henri-IV
evidence_summary: Patrick Modiano's entry into literature was catalyzed by Raymond Queneau, his geometry teacher at Lycée Henri-IV and a friend of his mother, who introduced him to the Gallimard publishing world. His childhood was marked by absent parents—his father involved in wartime black market dealings and his mother touring as an actress—and the death of his younger brother Rudy at age 9. These adversities, combined with his family's complex WWII history, shaped his obsessive literary focus on the Occupation period. His debut novel La Place de l'Étoile (1968), published at age 22, won the Fénéon Prize and Roger Nimier Prize.

name: Zico
milestone_by_age_26: Represented Brazil in the 1978 FIFA World Cup finishing third, and was voted South American Footballer of the Year in 1977 at age 24, while starring for Flamengo as their leading playmaker.
early_history_summary: Zico grew up in a working-class neighborhood of Rio de Janeiro and joined Flamengo's youth academy at age 14 in 1967 after scoring nine goals in a single match. He progressed through the youth ranks with 116 matches and 81 goals, making his professional debut in 1971 at age 18, and became a definitive starter by 1974. His older brothers were professional footballers, and he underwent an intensive physical development program at Flamengo to overcome his slight frame.
family_context_summary: Zico grew up in a working-class family of Portuguese descent in Quintino Bocaiuva, Rio de Janeiro. His older brothers Antunes and Edu were professional footballers, which provided early exposure to the sport and connections to clubs.
parent_family_domain_summary: Older brothers were professional footballers at América and other clubs; father José Antunes Coimbra was a fervent Flamengo supporter who encouraged Zico's trial at the club. Family domain immersion in football was significant.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Flamengo academy, football brothers, Rio de Janeiro, futsal, physical development program, working-class
evidence_summary: Zico grew up in a working-class Rio de Janeiro neighborhood with older brothers who were professional footballers, providing early domain immersion. He joined Flamengo's youth academy at 14 after scoring nine goals in a match, and progressed through 116 youth matches and 81 goals before his professional debut at 18 in 1971. Flamengo provided an intensive physical development program to build his slight frame. By 1974 he was a starter, and by 1977-78 he was voted South American Footballer of the Year and represented Brazil in the World Cup. His footballing environment in Rio and the Flamengo pipeline were the dominant early advantages.

name: Sigmar Polke
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded the Capitalist Realism art movement in May 1963 at age 22 with Gerhard Richter, Konrad Lueg, and Manfred Kuttner, staging their first exhibition in a vacant shop in Düsseldorf.
early_history_summary: Polke fled East Germany with his family in 1953, settling in West Germany. He worked as a stained glass apprentice in Düsseldorf before entering the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf in 1961 at age 20, where he studied under Karl Otto Götz, Gerhard Hoehme, and Joseph Beuys. In 1963, with fellow students Richter, Lueg, and Kuttner, he organized the first Capitalist Realism exhibition.
primary_leverage_engine: Artistic movement creation and academy network
family_context_summary: Polke was the seventh of eight children, born in Oels, Lower Silesia (now Poland). His family fled to Thuringia in 1945 during the expulsion of Germans after WWII, and escaped from East Germany to West Berlin in 1953, then to the Rhineland in West Germany.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No family artistic background is mentioned.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, Joseph Beuys, Gerhard Richter, Capitalist Realism, wartime displacement, Düsseldorf art scene
evidence_summary: Sigmar Polke's family was displaced by WWII, fleeing from Silesia to East Germany and then to West Germany in 1953. He began visiting galleries and working as a stained glass apprentice before entering the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf at age 20, where he met Gerhard Richter and Konrad Lueg. In 1963 at age 22, the group co-founded Capitalist Realism, organizing their first exhibition in a vacant Düsseldorf shop. The academy environment, peer network with Richter, and the post-war German cultural moment were the dominant early advantages. No family artistic background or financial privilege is documented.

name: Harvey Weinstein
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Harvey & Corky Productions in 1972 at age 20, promoting major rock concerts in Buffalo including Frank Sinatra, the Who, and the Rolling Stones, and took over the Century Theatre as a concert venue by 1974.
early_history_summary: Weinstein grew up in a Jewish family in Queens, New York, and attended SUNY Buffalo from 1969 to 1973. With fellow student Corky Burger, he began promoting rock concerts, starting with a successful 1972 Stephen Stills show. Harvey & Corky Productions became a fixture on the Buffalo music scene, bringing major acts to town and eventually taking over the Century Theatre as a concert venue.
family_context_summary: Weinstein grew up in a Jewish family in the Electchester housing co-op in Queens, New York. His father Max was a diamond cutter who died in 1976, and his mother Miriam (née Postel) died in 2016. His younger brother Bob became his business partner.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Father was a diamond cutter, not in entertainment or media. No family domain advantage in the film or music industry.
primary_early_advantage_tags: brother Bob, Corky Burger, SUNY Buffalo, concert promotion, Queens, self-created
evidence_summary: Harvey Weinstein grew up in a working-class Jewish family in Queens, with no entertainment industry connections. At SUNY Buffalo, he and fellow student Corky Burger began promoting rock concerts through the university activities board, founding Harvey & Corky Productions in 1972 after a successful Stephen Stills show. The business brought major acts to Buffalo and took over the Century Theatre as a venue. His brother Bob joined as a third partner, forming the team that would later create Miramax. The dominant early advantage was the complementary sibling/partner team and direct immersion in concert promotion.
